title: Ofsted Should Not Give Effort Grades
author: Andrew Old
summary: Andrew Old defends England's schools inspectorate against one persistent criticism, that Ofsted ratings correlate with a school's disadvantage and so are biased. He begins with a thought experiment: the same teacher will deliver a far better lesson to an eager class than to a hostile one, without being any worse a teacher, and the same is true of whole schools facing difficult intakes, recruitment problems or hostile communities. Ofsted's statutory job is to report on the quality of education provided, not the effort or heroism behind it, so a correlation with circumstances is expected rather than evidence of unfairness. Even if the remit were reopened, he argues, inspectors should keep giving the public accurate information, because hiding contextual gaps would conceal systemic inequality. Context can reasonably affect the consequences a school faces, but the answer to unfair outcomes is to reconsider those consequences, not to shoot the messenger.
points: The same teacher delivers very different lessons to easy and hostile classes, and Old argues the same logic applies to schools serving harder cohorts.
Ofsted's legal duty is the quality of education provided, so ratings that track circumstances are not by themselves a sign of bias.
Effort grades would reward the virtues of staff working in difficult schools but would stop telling parents and policymakers what education pupils actually receive.
Adjusting inspection findings for context would hide systemic inequalities that the system needs to see and address.
The better reform is to change what consequences follow a poor report in difficult circumstances, because accountability incentives currently encourage covering up problems.
quotes: Nevertheless, the quality of the education your pupils receive will be drastically different depending on factors entirely beyond your control.
It is unfortunate that, despite our good intentions, our best lessons may be delivered to the children who need them least, and our worst lessons may be delivered to those who most need to learn.
Schools may fail to provide a good education more due to external factors than internal ones.

Inspectors are judging what education pupils receive, not how impressive the school’s effort or contribution is. Their judgements are not biased or inaccurate simply because they show a correlation between the quality of education and the obstacles standing in the way of a high quality of education.
Perhaps it would be fairer if they gave “effort grades” that better reflected the virtues of the human beings working in schools that are up against it.
If it’s tough to provide a high quality education in “schools like these”, we don’t want a system that pretends it is happening anyway; we want one that addresses those difficulties.
The broader accountability framework creates incentives to cover up difficulties rather than address them.

It is reasonable to be concerned if you feel schools are “punished” for operating in difficult circumstances, but the answer must be to reconsider what happens to those schools, not to shoot the messenger.
